newsitem.title: USA: ANALYSTS SEE RECORD LARGE SOY CROP IN USDA REPORT.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEE RECORD LARGE SOY CROP IN USDA REPORT.

text.p: Tuesday's U.S. Agriculture Department crop production report will likely show a record large 1997/98 soybean crop but analysts said it was difficult to assess soy fields this early in the growing season.
"The August crop report is always a bit difficult," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney. "It's more of a population count than anything else and populations are pretty high this year."
A Reuter survey of analysts produced an average soybean production estimate of 2.68 billion bushels.
That figure was slightly below USDA's July outlook for 2.69 billion bushels. USDA will release its August crop production forecast on Tuesday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
Analysts noted USDA on June 30 pegged U.S. soybean plantings at a hefty 70.9 million acres, meaning even an average yield would produce a bumper crop.

Unusually dry weather last month in Illinois and Indiana may have trimmed yield potential but most analysts said soybeans can recover from weather stress in July. If problems linger in August then yields could deteriorate, they said.

Sid Love, analyst with Kropf/Love Consulting, pegged soybean output at 2.723 billion bushels, above the trade average. Love, who toured corn and soybean fields last week, said soybeans were tall and green and were holding up well despite the dry weather.
"We were impressed with the way the crop was holding on, waiting for moisture," Love wrote in comments prepared after the crop tour.

"The synergistic result of improved seed, better tillage, weed control, timely planting and maximum fertilizer usage all combined to produce a yield potential that needed only a modest boost from benign August weather to produce near record yields for both corn and soybeans," he added.
Near-record yields, combined with one of the largest planted areas on the books, would likely add up to a record crop, he said. Weather remains the wild card.
"The crop is on a teeterboard and yields can go up or down depending upon August rainfall," Love said.
ADM Investor Services analyst Steve Freed said it will be tough to summarize crop conditions and yield potentials because of differences in development and quality.

"Everybody in the eastern Corn Belt is using trendline yields and a lot of the crop is left (to develop)," said Steve Freed, analyst for ADM Investor Services. "In the western corn belt they're screaming record yields and the Delta/Southeast near trend or below."
"But the August 1 bean number is just a guess, especially with the dry areas," Freed added. "I wish we had another week, this makes it tough on analysts."

Merrill Lynch oilseeds analyst Mario Balletto said the trade will use Tuesday's numbers as a starting point but would not draw too many conclusions from the data because August is viewed as the critical soybean development month whereas the corn crop develops rapidly in June.
"You can count ears on corn (on August 1) but you don't have any pods to count for soybeans," he said. USDA on Monday said 38 percent of soybeans were setting pods as of August 2.
